title: RC Circuit Charging: Time Constant and Exponential Approach
hook: How does a capacitor charge through a resistor? Discover the exponential curve and the meaning of the time constant τ = RC.

equation.caption: Capacitor voltage during charging in a series RC circuit.

explorations.title: Effect of Time Constant
explorations.predict: If you double R, what happens to the time to reach 63% of V0?
explorations.observe: The curve rises more slowly; the time to reach 63% doubles.
explorations.why: τ = RC, so doubling R doubles τ. The exponential term e^{-t/τ} decays more slowly, so V(t) approaches V0 more gradually.

explorations.title: Voltage at One Time Constant
explorations.predict: What fraction of V0 is reached at t = τ?
explorations.observe: At t = τ, V = 6.32 V, which is 63.2% of 10 V.
explorations.why: V(τ) = V0(1 - e^{-1}) ≈ 0.632 V0, independent of R and C.

self_tests.name: Voltage at τ is 63.2% of V0

limitation: This model assumes an ideal voltage source, ideal resistor, and ideal capacitor with no parasitic resistance or inductance. It also assumes the capacitor is initially uncharged and the switch is closed at t=0.
misconception: Students often think the capacitor charges linearly or that it reaches full voltage after one time constant. In reality, it charges exponentially and only reaches about 63% after one τ, and it takes about 5τ to be considered fully charged.

claims.text: The time constant τ is the product of resistance and capacitance: τ = RC.
The capacitor voltage during charging follows V(t) = V0(1 - e^{-t/τ}).
After one time constant, the capacitor reaches approximately 63.2% of the supply voltage.
After five time constants, the capacitor is considered fully charged (over 99%).
In our simulation, we assume ideal components and an initially uncharged capacitor.

outcomes.outcome: Explain the meaning of the time constant τ = RC.
Sketch the exponential charging curve V(t) = V0(1 - e^{-t/τ}).
Calculate the voltage at t = τ and t = 5τ.
Verify that V(0) = 0 and V(τ) ≈ 0.632 V0.
